notes: Build first. Smallest complete corpus, sharpest contestation (Śaṅkara / Rāmānuja / Madhva / Tilak / Gandhi), cleanest licensing, and Devanāgarī combining marks already exercise grapheme alignment.
Zhu Xi's Jizhu was the imperial examination curriculum from 1313 to 1905 across China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam — one interpretive layer selecting a civilisation's governing class for six centuries.
The hardest case and therefore the most useful to design against: RTL, an immutable source text, and a tradition where translation is categorically secondary.
Chapters from Langton (c. 1227), verses from Estienne (1551) — stable across every translation since, which is exactly the property the Canonical Reference needs.

Added as the second Chinese work. Earns its place on the variant axis: the Mawangdui (168 BCE) and Guodian (c. 300 BCE) manuscripts differ from the received text, including a word changed by imperial naming taboo — the sharpest possible demonstration of the `variant` layer kind.

Added as the second Indian work. A corpus rather than a single book, so it takes a Bible-shaped reference grammar: a short code per Upaniṣad plus a numeric path. Śaṅkara commented on ten of them, which gives us the same commentator across two works — a real test of author-level layer navigation.

The seventh work, and the one that closes the largest hole in the corpus: six works covering Jewish, Christian, Islamic, Confucian, Daoist and Hindu reading, and no Buddhism — the most transnational tradition of all. Buddhaghosa's Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā is also a different SHAPE of commentary from anything else here: each verse gets a narrative occasion rather than a gloss, which stress-tests the layer model usefully.
